I think this is what Baumol’s cost disease is about (productivity growth on one sector drives up labor costs and ultimately prices in other sectors, such as healthcare, construction). Basically, when software or AI is super lucrative,

1. students go into new lucrative thing

2. supply of doctors goes down

3. doctor wages go up

4. hospital margins go down

5. Hospitals raise their prices to stay in business

6. Wealthy engineers are able to afford higher prices

7. Services that are transitively consumed by the high-productivity sector stabilize at a higher price. Services not transitively consumed by the high-productivity sector go out of business.

Baumol illustrated his point in a simple manner. In the 1700's a string quartet required four musicians, and today a string quartet still requires four musicians (no productivity gain). However, those musicians today expect 21st-century salaries to match the rest of the economy, making the cost of hiring a quartet vastly more expensive relative to goods like mass-produced items.

>...Is the cross-elasticity of demand here not referring specifically to the cross-elasticity of different forms of labor, which exists due to the many common inputs of different forms of labor?

This isn't necessary to explain Baumol cost disease. Different kinds of workers may also be substitutes for one another, or complements. However, the quartet doesn't need to share a particular set of inputs with car manufacturing for Baumol's mechanism to operate.

>...In the case of a quartet, if musicians charged what they did in 1700, they would quickly become homeless, and then quickly get other jobs.

Yes. Baumol cost disease is a way to explain the upward pressure on the cost of lower productivity labor-intensive services. It isn't an economic law, it is a tendency. It doesn't guarantee that every business will be able to pass those costs on to customers, or that every business will survive or that every worker will receive the same wage increase, etc.

Ok, I did more reading. I was actually super wrong about this, but it took me a while to get there. Oops! But very interesting!

Basically, people and firms are little black holes of unmet demand for all sorts of things. When the productivity shock happens, demand for stuff in the now-high-productivity sector(s) is now (mostly) met, freeing up money (that people and firms in the high-productivity sectors have more money to meet their own latent demand is also true, but somewhat incidental). That money goes to meeting other latent demand, some of which is for stuff in low-productivity sectors (housing, childcare, education, healthcare, construction), and that’s what drives up prices until/as people eventually move into those sectors. Even if housing specifically isn’t constrained, it still happens.

And I guess…as wages go up, some forms of automation also become economically sensible, which is what changes the balance of low/high productivity sectors. Latent demand for rope-holding is met with cones, latent demand for maids is (mostly) met with washing machines and dishwashers, latent demand for secretaries is (mostly) met with personal computers, etc.

So with AI, it sounds like people will move out of software into construction, healthcare, etc (only specialized work where the automation isn’t “good enough” stays). All the “teaching kids to code” that schools are doing now, eventually turns into people dealing with their own AI output as adults, where previously they would’ve hired a developer (like how managers who used to have a secretary now get a computer and type for themselves). Wages go up, education, healthcare, and housing get more expensive.
